title: Why can't anyone forecast this bar?
hook: A bar is fun with 60 people and awful with more. Everyone trusts one good forecast. Then?

knows: network effects make things more valuable as more people join
doesNotKnow: that with a crowding cost, any forecast everyone believes makes itself wrong

misconception: If everyone uses the same good forecast, the bar will be pleasantly busy.
objective: The learner can explain why a shared forecast of a crowded resource defeats itself (low sends everyone, high sends no one), and why even randomising leaves the bar crowded on nearly half the nights.

claims.text: If all 100 people act on the same forecast, all 100 come when it says 60 or fewer and nobody comes when it says more.
claims.source: The lesson's rule (each goes only if they expect 60 or fewer) applied to one shared forecast; Demo.tsx attendanceFor(): 50 → 100, 70 → 0.

claims.text: Any forecast everyone believes makes itself wrong.
claims.source: From c1: a believed forecast of 60 or fewer produces 100; a believed forecast above 60 produces 0; neither outcome matches the forecast.

claims.text: If each person goes independently with probability 0.6, attendance averages 60 and is above 60 on 46.2% of nights in the long run.
claims.source: Binomial(100, 0.6): mean 60; P(X > 60) = sum over k = 61..100 = 0.4621. Re-run in node by the builder (ncm-e02); matches the brief.

claims.text: The learner's own random nights show an average near 60 with a crowded share near half.
claims.source: Demo.tsx: mulberry32(1), 100 draws per night, each goes if r() < 0.6. Seed 1 was the first seed tried, not chosen for the result. Seed 1: 100 nights average 60.2, 48 crowded; 200 nights 60.3, 96 crowded. Seeds 2 and 3 at 100 nights: 38 and 44 crowded. The reveal quotes the learner's run.

claims.text: The average sits right at the limit, so nearly half the nights land above it.
claims.source: Mean 60 equals the limit; P(X > 60) = 0.462, P(X = 60) = 0.081, P(X < 60) = 0.457 for Binomial(100, 0.6).

claims.text: This is a model of Arthur's El Farol bar problem (1994): identical people, one shared forecast, no learning.
claims.source: W. B. Arthur, 'Inductive reasoning and bounded rationality', American Economic Review 84(2), 406-411 (1994; title and pages from memory). Model simplifications are the lesson's. The book chapter placement (Easley and Kleinberg 2010 ch. 17) is not cited to learners until the fact-checker confirms it. Fact-checker confirms attribution.

recall.question: A free museum is pleasant with up to 300 visitors. An app tells everyone '200 visitors expected today', and everyone believes it. What happens?
options: Far more than 300 come, because everyone expects room
recall.why: A believed low forecast sends everyone, which makes the forecast wrong. When more is worse, no forecast everyone trusts can be right.
